# Page 2^page=2
2 ADA COUNTY’S MAKING HISTORY AWARD To understand the present, we must understand the past Congratulations to local historian Barbara Perry Bauer on being selected by Ada County Development Services as this year’s recipient of the Making History Award. Barbara is a well-known historian who has worked on several projects in the Treasure Valley that have touched on every facet of Ada County’s rich history. She has researched and written about the streetcar systems that once connected the Treasure Valley’s communities. The award ceremony took place at Ivywild Park in Southeast Boise. Barbara has conducted extensive research on Ada County’s agricultural history and the role of irrigation in the development of the county and the Treasure Valley. Ada County is grateful for Barbara’s work in researching and telling the fascinating stories of Ada County’s past. Pictured L-R: Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley, Barbara Perry Bauer, and Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson Ivywild Park in Southeast Boise

# Page 3^page=3
3 ADA COUNTY’S PARK AT EXPO IDAHO Here’s how it’s going You see new pictures almost every week if you follow us on Facebook and other social media platforms. Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho is about seven months away from opening. This once-in-a-generation park is transforming an area of Ada County that has been a hub of activity for decades. You couldn’t ask for a better location; centrally located right alongside the Boise River with sweeping views of our precious Foothills. Just where is this new 42-acre park? It’s not in Boise. It’s not in Garden City and it’s not on private property. It’s right behind Ada County’s Expo Idaho property at the corner of Chinden Blvd. and Glenwood Street. (State Hwy 26 and State Hwy 44) It’s directly behind where you attend the Western Idaho Fair every year. The entire Expo Idaho Property is actually part of what’s called Unincorporated Ada County – surrounded by Garden City. Subscribe to Ada County’s YouTube and watch our regular progress videos. ADA COUNTY YOUTUBE - GREAT VIDEOS The drone footage gives you an amazing vantage point and illustrates just how vast this area is.

4 This project funded, in whole or in part, by the American Rescue Plan Act awarded to Ada County by the U.S. Department of Treasury. IMPORTANT: PLEASE SEND THIS TO SOMEONE YOU KNOW WHO MAY QUALIFY! Idaho’s Property Tax Reduction (or “Circuit Breaker”) program offers up to $1,500 in reductions for eligible homeowners with a 2025 income of $39,130 or less. Applicants must own a primary home, meet specific status requirements (age 65+, disabled, or widow/er), and apply between January 1 and April 15, 2026. The Idaho 100% Service-Connected Disabled Veteran Property Tax Benefit reduces primary residence property taxes by up to $1,500 for qualified veterans. This program is not income-restricted and is available to those rated 100% service-connected disabled or paid at the 100% rate due to individual unemployability by the VA as of January 1. Apply online through the Idaho State Tax Commission website or find the application and additional information on Ada County Assessor’s Office website. The deadline to apply is April 15, 2026 https://adacounty.id.gov/assessor/tax-relief-programs/circuit-breaker-tax-reduction/

# Page 5^page=5
5 ADA COUNTY VICTIM SERVICE CENTER Community Partner of the Year The Ada County Commissioners are proud to recognize Director Trina Allen and the Ada County Victim Services Center for being named Community Partner of the Year by Family Advocates. The Ada County Victim Services Center (ACVSC) in downtown Boise is a unique and critically important facility. The ACVSC is a one-stop location for anyone experiencing interpersonal violence. When you or someone you love walks through the door you have access to the center’s specialized multi-disciplinary team. As the Center marks its 20th year, this honor reflects the compassion, professionalism, and dedication Trina and her team bring to supporting victims and families across our community. Their work ensures people facing abuse and violence have access to the advocacy and resources they need during some of the most difficult moments in their lives. Learn more about the center: https://adacounty.id.gov/ victimservices/ Pictured L-R: Holly Koole, Chief of Staff; Heather McCarthy, Chief Civil Deputy; Michele Bandy, Deputy Director ACVSC; Jan Bennetts, Ada County Prosecutor; Trina Allen, Executive Director ACVSC; Maggi Thompson, Family Advocates; Scott Bandy, Chief Criminal Deputy Prosecutor ADA COUNTY GOVERNMENT In addition to elected offices, Ada County government includes twelve individual departments. Each department provides important services to our residents in Star, Eagle, Meridian, Boise, Garden City, Kuna, and Unincorporated Ada County. These services include law enforcement protection, emergency preparedness, election services, parks & waterways, indigent services, juvenile services, solid waste management, the Western Idaho Fair, Weed, Pest & Mosquito Abatement and more. Learn more about the services provided to you by Ada County - www.adacounty.id.gov/

7 PROCUREMENT MONTH – MARCH 2026 Ada County is recognizing the skilled professionals who secure the maximum value for each tax dollar – Ada County Procurement! Ada County Procurement’s responsibilities include guiding individuals through the procurement process, maintaining ethical and impartial relations with vendors, and assisting with the budget process. The Ada County Procurement team ensures that decentralized programs have centralized controls by creating rules and regulations for purchasing that are in the County’s best interest and ensure compliance with Idaho Code. The support and advice Procurement offers on capital projects and acquisitions are an integral part of our County’s growth and development. Thank you for your outstanding service to Ada County! Pictured L-R: Robyn Swaney, Procurement Officer II; Evan Amidan, Procurement Officer II; Jack Burns, Buyer; Alyssa Ellington, Procurement Manager; Bob Perkins, Procurement Director; Ken Sinclair, Fleet Manager; Olga Tymoshchuk, Procurement Officer I; Kathy Corless, Procurement Analyst

8 ADA COUNTY PROCUREMENT’S 20TH ANNUAL VENDOR FAIR Ada County employees had the chance to connect with a wide range of vendors, explore innovative products and services, and learn about the latest in office equipment, workplace solutions, and environmentally friendly products. “The 20th Annual Ada County Vendor Fair is an opportunity for local businesses to showcase their goods and services to Ada County Offices and Departments,” said Ada County Procurement Director Bob Perkins. “This event kicks off the budget season and helps offices and departments with budgeting for the upcoming fiscal year. Many of the participating vendors are on Cooperative Contracts that provide competitive pricing for their goods and services.” A big thank you to Ada County Procurement for all of their hard work making this a great event again this year. Thank you to all of the vendors who participated and helped make this event such a success. Congratulations to the raffle prize winners! We appreciate everyone who stopped by and helped make today a great event. We’re already looking forward to next year! By: Billy Kidd Ada County Communications

9 We love sharing Ada County’s story! Thank you to the Rotary Club of Boise Sunrise for inviting Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley to speak to this early bird group on Tuesday, March 10th. Commissioner Dayley explained the role of county commissioners in Idaho and the importance of understanding how county government works, and how it directly affects your life. IDAHO’S OFFICIAL AMERICA 250 AMBASSADOR BAND SHARES “FOREVER IDAHO” If you’re new to Idaho, or if your family has lived here for generations, this song captures perfectly what makes Idaho and Idahoans so extraordinary. “Forever Idaho” was formally recognized by both the Idaho Senate and the Idaho House of Representatives as the official song for Idaho’s America 250 celebrations. Written by two Idaho songwriters, Forever Idaho honors our state’s people, heritage, and enduring spirit. Thank you to Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth for sharing this video, and for the enormous amount of work you and your staff are doing to make the 250th anniversary of the Signing of the Declaration of Independence so special. Idaho is celebrating in style! FOREVER IDAHO - IDAHO’S OFFICIAL A250 SONG

# Page 10^page=10
10 It means I can choose to go to church on the Sabbath with my family—or go to the park with my dog on Sunday—or do both, or neither. It means I can speak up, or I can stay silent. It means I can own a gun and drive a Ford truck or own a bike and drive a Subaru. It means I can listen to rock, pop, classical, gospel, or country music—or all the above. It means I can choose to play soccer, football, or run track—or I can play the tuba, play Dungeons & Dragons, or join the chess club. It means I can start voting when I am 18 and decide who represents me when making or enforcing laws—or I can grow old and never vote and just complain about how politicians I didn’t choose aren’t doing a good job. I can live in California and blame all my problems on Iowa or live in Iowa and blame all my problems on New York. Or I could live in Idaho, choose to be happy and not blame anyone for my position in life. I can order a Big Mac, fries, and a vanilla shake, or choose a salad, a cup of soup, and an apple. I can go skiing in the mountains at night or watch a movie on my phone in bed. I can, through hard work and determination, improve my circumstances in life—or I can choose doom- scrolling through my social media feeds. I can join the military and salute the flag every time I see it, or I can choose to never fly the flag. It means I can choose to be a firefighter, a lawyer, a bus driver, an accountant, or a thousand other things—because where there is a will, there is a way, thanks to the Declaration of Independence. It means I am free to choose. It also means I am free from tyranny—that I am not subject to a king, but to laws established by my fellow citizens. It means I will be fairly judged by my peers if I choose not to follow those laws. It means the military is dedicated to defending me and my rights, not attacking me, or stripping me of them. It means I am not subject to taxes unless I have fair representation in establishing them. It is important to remember that forcing someone else to act, live, or believe a certain way was the very reason the Declaration of Independence was written and signed. I may not choose to act, live, or believe like someone next to me, but I will fight just as hard for them to retain their rights as I do for my own. It is my hope that as we celebrate 250 years of freedom, we look outward and remember to respect those freedoms for all citizens—not turn inward and focus only on what benefits ourselves. As a member of the military for 25 years, I traveled all around the world. America was a beacon of hope—a bright light on a hill. It represented a dream for so many people who do not enjoy the same freedoms. I know we don’t always get it right—we are not perfect—but I could clearly see that I was blessed with freedoms many people do not have. It is my hope now that we can all pause and reflect on the good things we have because of the Declaration of Independence, and celebrate those things—as a people, as neighbors, as families, and as brothers and sisters in this great cause of freedom in this amazing country, the United States of America.

# Page 11^page=11
11 CONGRATULATIONS BRYAN GILBERT ON 20 YEARS OF SERVICE Bryan brought his experience to Ada County on March 20, 2006, when he joined Development Services as a Building Inspector. In this role, he applied his field knowledge to ensure compliance with building codes and to help safeguard the health and safety of our local community one inspection at a time. Bryan was promoted to Building Plans Examiner in 2017, where he transitioned from inspecting construction to reviewing building plans. In this capacity, he worked closely with contractors, engineers, and design professionals to ensure projects met all applicable codes and standards before construction began. In recognition of his leadership, technical expertise, and commitment to public service, Bryan was promoted to Ada County Building Official on December 20, 2021. In this role, he has taken on key responsibilities overseeing building code enforcement, supporting building staff, and helping guide construction and development throughout Ada County. Bryan’s commitment to professional excellence is reflected in the 13 International Code Council (ICC) certifications he holds, demonstrating both his technical expertise and dedication to continual learning. Outside of his professional career, Bryan has demonstrated remarkable dedication to the sport or martial art of judo, with more than 50 years of involvement as a competitor, coach, referee and recognized second-degree black belt sensei. His long-standing commitment to the sport reflects the same discipline, leadership, and mentorship he brings to his work. Bryan’s unique combination of hands-on construction experience, technical expertise, and leadership has made a lasting impact on Ada County Development Services and the community it serves – and it is our privilege to recognize Bryan Gilbert for 20 years of dedicated service to Ada County. Ada County Development Services Staff gather to congratulate Bryan!

# Page 12^page=12
12 JAKE OVEN 25 YEARS Like many people in EMS, Jake Oven’s contribution to Ada County Paramedics comes without much fanfare. He works purposefully and efficiently to further our cause. That work ethic is evident in a variety of ways. One day Jake might be involved in the planning of a special event and then be working that event the next day. After that, he might be drafting specifications for our next ambulance purchase, a vital role in our organization. The next day, Jake might be working in the field leading a battalion of medics and EMTs, a difficult job Jake mastered years ago. Mixed in, you’ll find Jake participating and contributing to many other aspects of our business and operation. We can count on Jake to have specific ideas that mix well with his higher-level perspective. Of all the words one might use to describe Jake, stalwart springs to mind. His hardworking dedication to Ada County Paramedics can’t help but be seen, and our organization is, on a daily basis, much better off with Jake’s contributions. Thank you very much for 25 years of service to ACP and the citizens of Ada County Pictured L-R: Captain Cameo Rogers; Sue Peterson, Jake’s mom; Paramedic Candice Oven, Jake’s wife; Battalion Chief Jake Oven; Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck; Ada County Paramedics Chief John Blake; Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson and Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley
